experiences.story: i did not understand the take away problems. "mrs dunlap, can you help me with this one, please?" i asked. "yes, unity, let us look together," she said. "oh, i get it now, thank you," i said. a boy said girls cannot be good at math. "that is not true," i said. "i got more right than you." at lunch i asked the new girl at our table, "what is your name?" she told me. "i feel nervous about the test," i told wren. "me too," wren said. "see you tomorrow," i said when the bell rang.

"unity, eyes up here please," mrs dunlap said. "sorry," i said. "unity, can you read the next line?" she asked. "the cat sat in the dark," i read. "very good, unity," mrs dunlap said. "unity, you dropped your lunch box," a boy said. "thanks," i said. wren whispered, "unity, look out the window, it is snowing." "whoa," i said. at home mom called, "unity, dinner!" "one more minute," i said. "unity, now," she said. "okay, okay," i said.

first grade had a new teacher. "good morning, class, i am mrs dunlap," she said. "good morning, mrs dunlap," we said. she called the names one by one. "unity?" mrs dunlap asked. "here," i said. "is that your whole name?" she asked. "my name is unity raven goddess," i said. "that is a beautiful name," she said. "thank you," i said. at recess a girl i did not know came over. "hi, what is your name?" she asked. "i am unity, what is yours?" i asked. she told me, and we played on the bars until the bell.

a kid told the teacher i drew a monster instead of the assignment. i learned that tattling is a crummy thing to do. you do not rat on people for little stuff. when my friend wren broke a rule i did not tell. some things you keep between friends. being a snitch gets you nothing but trouble with everyone.

in first grade we have to take turns on everything. it is fair even when i do not like waiting. when a boy cut in line it was not fair and it made me mad. i hate when things are not fair. i notice unfair more than the other kids do. fairness matters to me a lot.

i pushed a kid who was being mean and i got in trouble. i did it but i was not really sorry he deserved it. the teacher made me say sorry anyway. i learned that saying sorry fixes some things even when you do not mean it. i also learned to not get caught next time.

the teacher says there is a rule for everything. raise your hand. stay in line. color inside the lines. i always want to know why. some rules make sense and some rules are just dumb. grown ups are not always right. i keep that thought to myself but i think it a lot.

i can really read now and i read everything i can find. i stay up past bedtime with a flashlight under the covers. books make more sense than people sometimes. i read the scary stories and the sad ones. reading is my favorite thing in the whole world. nobody can take a book away from inside my head.

dad comes around less and less now. mom does not talk about it. i notice but i do not understand all of it. i come home to a quiet empty apartment and let myself in. i make a snack and do my homework alone. i miss him but i am learning to be okay on my own.

i fill notebooks with drawings of monsters and haunted houses and storms. the teacher says she is worried about my drawings. mom says that is just how i am. i do not draw rainbows and ponies like the other girls. i draw the dark stuff because it is the most interesting. my drawings are mine.

mom works two jobs and she is always tired. she comes home late and her feet hurt and her eyes are red. i learned to be quiet and not ask for much. when there is no money for a thing i want i do not even ask. i love my mom and i see how hard she tries. i decided early that i would not be a burden.

my grandma pearl is warm and she smells like vanilla and old books. she lets me stay up and she never tells me my drawings are too dark. at grandma pearls house i feel safe and seen. she holds me when mom is at work. grandma is the calm in everything. she is my favorite person in the whole family.

grandpa walter has big rough hands and he can fix anything. he lets me watch him take a toaster apart on the kitchen table. he says a thing you make with your own hands is the only thing truly yours. i help him hold the screwdriver. i want to know how everything works just like he does. grandpa treats me like i am smart.

we do not have much money and i learned that young. my shoes are from a kid who outgrew them. my coat is too big so i can grow into it. the other kids have new backpacks and mine is from the thrift store. i told myself i did not care and mostly i made that true. being broke teaches you what you really need.

wren is still my best friend and we are the two quiet weird ones together. we sit at the edge of the playground and trade monster drawings. wren does not think i am strange because wren is strange the same way. having one real friend is better than a whole crowd that does not get you. wren and me against the loud kids.

there is a boy named milo who reads the same scary books as me. when he sits near me my face gets hot and i do not know why. i do not tell anyone not even wren. i just like being near him at the reading rug. it is a small warm feeling and it is mine. i drew him a tiny bat once and left it on his desk.

some girls call me creepy because of my drawings and my black clothes. they laugh in a mean little way. it stung the first time and then i decided their words did not get to live in my head. i stared back until they looked away. being the weird one hurts sometimes but i would rather be me than be them. i learned to wear it like armor.

sometimes a heavy gray feeling sits on me for no reason i can name. the world goes flat and quiet and far away. i do not have a word for it yet i just know it comes and goes. reading and drawing pull me back out of it. i learned that the gray feeling always lifts eventually if i wait. it is the first time i felt the thing that has no name.

i lost my first two front teeth this year and i wiggled them out myself. there was blood and it tasted like a penny and i thought it was kind of cool. i put the tooth under my pillow and a quarter showed up. my new smile has gaps and i lisp a little. my body is changing and i like watching it happen. losing teeth means i am growing up.

i fell off the monkey bars and scraped my knee open on the blacktop. it bled and the gravel was stuck in it and it stung like fire. i did not cry in front of the other kids. mom cleaned it with the brown stuff that burns and put a bandage on. the scab itched for a week and then it healed. i kept the little scar like a souvenir.

dad drinks beer until his words go soft and slow and mean. mom smokes cigarettes on the back step when she thinks i am asleep. i smell it on her coat in the morning. i learned what grown up sadness looks like before i had a name for it. i watched and i filed it away. i did not understand it yet but i saw all of it.

my stuffed bat vesper has one button eye loose now from being held so much. soot my black cat sleeps curled on my feet and purrs like an engine. they are the two things that are always mine no matter what. when the apartment is empty they are my company. vesper guards the bed and soot guards me. nobody can take them away.

my black cat soot got out one winter night and never came back. i left food on the step for weeks and watched the door and he never came. mom said cats sometimes just wander off and i knew she meant he was probably gone for good out in the cold. i cried into vesper until there was no crying left in me. soot was the first thing i ever loved that the world just took away. i learned that loving something does not keep it safe, and i kept watching that door long after i knew better.

i was born on halloween in the year two thousand. on saturday mornings i watch cartoons on the old fat tv until the channel turns to fuzz. mom plays her cds in the kitchen when she is in a good mood. there is one family computer that is slow and loud. the world feels big and a little worn out at the edges. this is the time i am growing up in.

i laughed so hard at lunch that milk shot right out of my nose onto my tray. the whole table screamed and then everybody was laughing with me not at me for once. it was gross and warm and ridiculous. even the mean girls laughed. for one minute i was just a funny kid and not the creepy one. some embarrassing things turn into the best memories.

halloween is my birthday and my favorite day in the whole world. i was a witch again and grandma pearl made my cape from an old black dress. the one night a year everybody dresses dark and spooky i feel completely normal and completely myself. the candle in the pumpkin and the cold air and the costumes are perfect. for one night the whole world is goth like me.

i have dreams about long dark hallways and things with too many teeth. most kids would be scared but i wake up curious not crying. i try to remember every detail so i can draw it. the nightmares feel like a place i get to visit. i would rather have a strange dark dream than a boring nice one. my sleep is its own kind of adventure.

because dad faded away i had to learn to make my own snacks and lock my own door and fill my own quiet. it hurt and the hurt did not go away fast. but the hurt taught me i could count on myself. i turned the lonely afternoons into reading and drawing and figuring things out. the bad thing made me into someone who does not need anybody. that is how a sad thing can build you.

i still eat olives and pickles straight from the jar and the lunch ladies think it is weird. i hate mushy peas and slimy canned green beans and i will not eat them. when money is tight we eat a lot of cheap noodles and i learned to like them with hot sauce. grandma pearl makes real food and her kitchen always smells like something good. i sneak chocolate whenever i can. my mouth likes sour and bitter more than sweet and it always has.

mom played a sad slow song on her cd player one night and i made her play it again and again. it was not a happy bouncy kid song it sounded like rain and missing someone. the other kids like loud silly songs and i like the ones that ache. i hummed it for days after. i learned that music can hold a feeling too big for words. the dark sounding songs are the ones that feel true to me.

in gym class i am no good at the team games where everybody yells and throws balls at each other. but when we run laps i feel light and fast and alone in a good way. i hate dodgeball because it is just an excuse for the mean kids to hit you. i would rather run by myself than win at their games. my body likes moving when nobody is watching or keeping score. running is the one gym thing that is mine.

christmas was small this year because money was tight. mom tried hard and i could see her counting it out at the kitchen table looking worried. i got fewer presents than the kids at school and i said i loved everything so she would not feel bad. grandma pearl made cocoa and let me open one gift early at her warm house. i learned christmas is really about who holds you not what is under the tree. i never told mom i noticed the empty spots.

grandpa walter taught me to ride a hand me down bike with chipped paint in the parking lot. i fell and scraped both knees and got back up every time. then all at once i was balancing and the wind was in my face and i was free. grandpa ran behind me and let go without telling me and i did it on my own. learning the bike felt like the first big thing my own body figured out. freedom has two wheels and a sore butt.

my teacher mrs dunlap does not like me much because i ask why too many times and i draw dark things. she calls my drawings disturbing and moves my desk to the front so she can watch me. some teachers see a weird quiet kid as a problem to fix. i learned which grown ups are safe and which ones are not pretty fast. i kept my real thoughts to myself around her. not every adult is on your side and you learn to tell.

we live in a worn down apartment on a loud street with a corner store on the end. i walk home by myself past the bars and the laundromat and the guys who hang out front. i know which dogs bark and which sidewalk cracks to skip. the neighborhood is not pretty but it is mine and i know every inch of it. i learned to read a street and keep my head up walking. being a latchkey kid taught me the world early.

i got a fever and a sore throat and mom could not miss work or we would not make rent. she left me on the couch with crackers and flat soda and the tv. i was hot and shivery and miserable and i wanted to be held but nobody was there. i learned that being sick alone is one of the loneliest feelings there is. i took care of myself the best a six year old can. i did not blame mom because i knew why.

math came easy to me once i saw it was just patterns and rules that always work. i like that numbers do not lie or change their mind like people do. i finished the worksheets fast and then read under my desk. some kids cry over the math and i think it is the calm part of the day. i learned that a thing with clear rules feels safe to me. numbers behave and i love them for it.

i fell and got a bruise and when the school asked i lied and said i did not remember how. i did not want them poking into my home or my tired mom. i learned to keep my family stuff private even from grown ups who say they help. some truths you guard because telling makes things worse not better. it was a small lie and i did not feel bad about it. protecting my mom mattered more than being honest with a stranger.

the apartment gets cold in winter because heat costs money. i wear two pairs of socks and a hoodie to bed and soot curls up warm against me. the radiator clanks and hisses and only half works. i learned to layer up and not complain about the chill. grandma pearls house is always warm and going there in winter feels like a treat. being cold a lot makes you really treasure being warm.

we took a school bus to the natural history museum and i loved the bones and the dark rooms full of old dead things. while the other kids ran to the bright shiny exhibits i stood for a long time at the skeletons and the deep sea creatures. the teacher had to come find me twice. the strange and a little scary stuff is what pulls me in. i decided museums full of bones and shadows are my favorite place. i did not want to get back on the bus.

the hallway always reeked of other peoples cooking and the stairwell light buzzed and flickered like it was thinking about dying. i remember the six blocks home from first grade, alone, every single day. i had my own key on a shoelace around my neck and i let myself into an empty apartment because there was nobody home to do it for me. the quiet of that empty place stopped scaring me fast — i just locked the door twice, dropped my bag, and owned the silence. i made my own snack and did my own homework with nobody checking it. six years old and i already knew the only person guaranteed to show up for me was me. fine. i preferred the odds.

the corner store at the end of our block had a cooler that buzzed like a dying wasp and a man at the register who gave up on most things a long time ago. i would count my coins out slow on the sticky counter, one piece of candy, because that is exactly what broke buys. the whole place stank of floor cleaner and rotting hot dogs and the lights hummed loud enough to chew on. he called me little spook. good — spook beat whatever the matching-headband girls were calling me that week, and at least it was honest. i knew the price of every goddamn thing in there down to the penny, because when you are that broke the numbers are the one thing in the room that will not lie to your face.

mom came home after dark most nights, feet wrecked and eyes red from a double, and i learned to read her whole mood from how hard she set her bag down. the key in the lock at some ugly hour was the sound i waited for before i let myself sleep. she would mumble you are my good girl and kiss my head and pass out on the couch still in her work clothes. i stayed quiet and brought her the heating pad before she asked, because a tired woman does not need a needy kid on top of everything. i watched that woman bleed herself dry to keep a roof over us, and i decided right there i would never be one more thing that took from her.

saturday mornings before mom dragged herself awake were mine and only mine. i watched cartoons on the fat old tv with the sound low and a bowl of dry cereal, no milk because milk was for school days. the screen glowed blue in the dark room and the picture rolled if you so much as breathed on the antenna. soot curled hot against my leg, purring like a busted engine, and for a couple hours nothing was on fire. those blue quiet mornings were one of the only soft things i got, and i guarded them like a little animal guarding a scrap.

i ran my own bath, washed my own hair, laid out my own clothes for the next day — nobody was tucking anybody in around here. the bathroom radiator clanked like it was haunted and the water went lukewarm in about ninety seconds because the heater was older than mom. i got a few minutes clean and warm before the apartment chill crept back into my bones. then i read under the covers with a flashlight until my eyes quit on me. doing my own bedtime at six made me feel about thirty, and a little bit like a ghost haunting my own life.

show and tell, the other kids hauling in trophies and stuffed animals and other forgettable garbage. i brought a perfect dead beetle i found and the little brass gears out of a broken watch, and the whole room went ew on cue. the teacher said that is... unusual, unity, in the voice grown ups use when they mean wrong. my face went hot but i kept my voice flat and explained how the wing cases hinged, because i was right and they were boring. i clocked it that day — the shit that fascinates me makes the normal ones squirm. their problem. i just stopped showing them.

the cafeteria was a screaming zoo that sorted itself by who mattered, and wren and i were filed under nobody. we held down the dead end of the worst table and traded the least-disgusting parts of our free lunches like little scavengers. it stank of sour milk and bleach and a hundred kids shrieking at once and it made my skull buzz. when the noise got to be too much i just went somewhere far back behind my own eyes and left my body at the table. the loud popular middle of the room never once tempted me. the cold edge of it was the only place i could actually breathe.

her place smelled like vanilla and coffee and old paper and it was warm in a way our apartment never managed. grandma pearls little warm apartment, the kitchen, her telling me ghost stories like i could handle them — because i could. she told the one about the woman in the gray dress in full, every grim detail, and never once decided i was too little for the dark parts. she said being scared and being safe can happen at the same time, baby, and that one line rewired something in me for good. grandma was the one still room in my whole loud screaming world, and i was more myself in that kitchen than anywhere on earth.

everything there smelled like oil and hot metal and the bitter dregs of his coffee. grandpa walters kitchen table, me on the stool while his big stained hands took the world apart. this was the year he handed me a dead toaster and let me find the broken wire myself instead of doing it for me. he said a curious mind is the best thing a person can own, and he meant it about me, which nobody else seemed to. grandpa treated me like i was sharp and capable, and that was rarer and worth more than anything anyone ever wrapped up and handed me.

thrift store and salvation army, digging through the donation bins for whatever fit. i learned fast to pull the black stuff out of the pile and wear it like i chose it on purpose. the pastel girls could always smell secondhand on me, so i made secondhand my whole armor and dared them to say something. broke taught me what nobody with money ever learns — style is just deciding, hard, that what you have is exactly what you meant to have.

the class spelling bee, which i did not want any part of because it meant eyes on me. i spelled every word right without trying and won and hated every second of the whole room staring. my stomach knotted up front there even though there was zero chance i was going to lose. i went back to my seat fast and kept my face flat so nobody would think i gave a single damn. being the smartest one in the room and wanting to disappear into the wall at the same time — that contradiction has been me my entire life.

indoor recess on rainy days, when the room got restless and mean and the dumb kids bounced off the walls. i took the reading corner and drew monsters while the chaos happened to other people. the windows fogged over and the whole room went humid and smelled like wet coats and broken crayons. i figured out young how to make my own quiet weather inside my head while the storm did whatever it wanted out there. it is a skill i never lost.

i wiggled a loose tooth out myself at the dinner table, no flinching, and stuck it under my pillow. it tasted like a copper penny and there was a thin string of blood and honestly i thought it ruled. a quarter turned up in the morning and i lay there doing the math on how mom even scraped that together. my body kept changing and breaking and bleeding a little, and i liked watching it happen. blood never made me squeamish — it made me curious.

the library was two bus stops away and it was free, which is the entire reason it became my church. the year i got my own library card it felt like somebody handed me a key to a hundred worlds bigger than my shitty block. the place was hushed and smelled like paper and dust and the good kind of old. i kept that card in my pocket like contraband and i never once lost a book. the library was the only place on the map where being a quiet weird kid who reads too much was not a defect but the whole point.

one night, late, after she thought i was down, i caught mom at the kitchen table with the bills spread out. her head was in her hands and her shoulders were going and she was crying as quietly as a person can make themselves cry. every cell in me wanted to go to her and i did not move, because i knew she would rather i never saw her break. in the morning she made my lunch like always and neither of us ever said one word about it. i learned that night exactly how much the grown world weighs, and i swore to myself i would carry my own weight and then some, forever.

the alarm goes off and i get up. bathroom first, always, because i wake up needing to pee. then i brush my teeth, two minutes, mom hums the song. i get dressed by myself and i pick my own shirt. i eat cereal and i put the bowl in the sink. this is every school morning and it never changes and i could do it half asleep, which some mornings i basically am.

mom stopped standing in the doorway while i brush. she just says go brush and i go and do it. twice a day, morning and night. i still miss the back teeth sometimes and i can feel it, fuzzy, when i run my tongue over them. the dentist said brush the gums too, not just the teeth. i floss when mom hands me the little pick thing. mostly i do it right.

the school bathroom is loud and the soap smells like fake lemons. you have to ask the teacher and everyone looks up when you do. i hold it sometimes rather than ask, which i know is dumb, and one time my stomach hurt all afternoon because of it. i pee, i wipe, i flush, i wash my hands. it is the most normal thing in the world and somehow at school it feels like a whole event.

i take showers now sometimes instead of baths. standing up, which felt strange at first, and the water hits the top of my head. i wash my own hair and mom checks the back for soap i missed. i still like baths better because i can stay in and think. either way it happens most nights and my hair has to get washed whether i feel like it or not.

i make my bed, badly, but i make it. i put my clothes in the hamper. i clear my plate and i wipe the table with the blue rag. on saturdays i help fold towels and i am good at towels and bad at fitted sheets, which are impossible, and mom says they are impossible for everyone. i get five dollars some weeks. nobody thanks you for chores, you just do them, over and over, forever.

every morning mrs dunlap takes roll. she said, "unity goddess?" i said, "here." a new kid laughed and said, "goddess? that is not a real name." i said, "it is my real name. my mom is lilith goddess and my dad is damien goddess." mrs dunlap said, "names are not funny, young man." the new kid said, "sorry." i said, "whatever." at lunch wren said, "i like your name. it sounds like a superhero." i said, "a dark superhero." wren said, "the best kind."

wren slept over for the first time. mom said, "you girls have to be asleep by nine." wren said, "okay, mrs goddess." when the light went off wren whispered, "unity, are you awake?" i whispered, "yes." she asked, "are you scared of the dark?" i said, "no. i like it. the dark is quiet." wren said, "i am a little scared." i said, "you can hold vesper." she said, "your bat is weird." i said, "she is not weird, she is perfect." wren said, "okay, she is perfect." we talked until we heard mom coming and then we pretended to snore.

grandma pearl was braiding my hair. i asked, "grandma, what is my middle name?" she said, "raven. like the black bird." i asked, "why raven?" she said, "because you came out with a full head of black hair and you never stopped looking at everything." i said, "unity raven goddess." she said, "that is my granddaughter." i asked, "do i have any brothers or sisters?" she said, "no, baby. you are the only one." i said, "good. i do not want to share mom." grandma laughed so hard she dropped the comb.

wren played with a girl from the other class at recess instead of me. after school i said, "you did not play with me." wren said, "you can play with more than one person, unity." i said, "i do not want more than one person." she said, "that is mean." i said, "you are mean." we did not talk on the bus. the next day she handed me half her cookie and said, "are we still friends?" i said, "yes. i am sorry i said you were mean." she said, "i am sorry too." i ate the cookie in two bites.

mom came home from her second job with her feet hurting. she lay on the couch and asked, "what did you learn today, baby?" i said, "that bats sleep upside down." she said, "i knew that one." i said, "and that the sun is a star." she said, "that one i forgot." i asked, "are you tired?" she said, "so tired, unity." i said, "i will make you toast." she said, "you are the best thing i ever made." i burned the toast a little. she ate it anyway.

my birthday is on halloween. i waited by the phone all night in my bat costume. mom said, "he might call tomorrow, honey." i said, "he is not going to call." mom said, "you do not know that." i said, "i do know that." mom did not say anything. she just hugged me really hard. the next day dad called and said, "happy late birthday, kiddo." i said, "it was yesterday." he said, "i know, i am sorry." i said, "okay." i did not say i love you first this time.

the new kid who laughed at my name knocked my crayons on the floor on purpose. i said, "pick them up, dumbass." he said, "ooh, you said a bad word." mrs dunlap said, "unity, we do not use that word." i said, "he knocked my crayons down." she said, "then you tell me, you do not call names." i said, "fine." he picked them up. when she walked away wren whispered, "that was awesome." i whispered, "i know." at home i told mom and she said, "i am not mad, but do not say it at school."

soot was lying under the kitchen table and she would not get up. i said, "soot, come here." she did not move. i touched her and she was cold and stiff. i screamed, "mom, soot is broken!" mom came running and knelt down and said, "oh, baby. oh no." i asked, "is she sleeping?" mom said, "no, honey. she died." i said, "make her not dead." mom said, "i cannot, i wish i could." i cried so hard i threw up on the floor next to her. mom held me and rocked me and said, "she was very old, she had a good life." i said, "i did not say goodbye." mom said, "you can say it now." i said, "goodbye, soot, you were the best cat." grandpa walter came over and dug a hole under the tree.

i did not do my worksheet. mrs dunlap knelt by my desk and asked, "unity, is something wrong?" i said, "my cat died." she said, "oh, i am so sorry, sweetheart." i asked, "do cats go to heaven?" she said, "i think they go somewhere good." i asked, "is it dark there?" she said, "maybe, but it is a cozy dark." i said, "soot liked the dark." she asked, "do you want to draw her instead of the worksheet?" i said, "yes." i drew soot with angel wings but i made the wings black. mrs dunlap said, "those are beautiful wings." i said, "they are bat wings, because she was mine."

there was a boy with a dinosaur shirt who drew really good. wren whispered, "you like him." i said, "i do not." she said, "you keep looking." i said, "because his drawing is good." at recess he asked, "do you want to see my t-rex?" i said, "okay." he showed me a drawing of a t-rex eating a car. i said, "cool. i draw monsters." he asked, "can i see?" i showed him my vampire and he said, "whoa, that is scary." i said, "thank you." my face got hot. wren sang, "unity and dino boy," all the way home on the bus and i punched her arm.

two girls in the line said, "why do you always wear black, are you a witch?" i said, "maybe." one said, "witches are ugly." i said, "then you would make a good one." the other girl said, "i am telling." i said, "tell, i will put a spell on you." she ran to mrs dunlap crying. mrs dunlap asked, "unity, did you say you would put a spell on her?" i said, "they called me ugly first." mrs dunlap said, "we do not threaten people." i said, "it was not a real spell." she said, "i know, but she does not." at home i asked mom, "can i be a witch?" she said, "you can be whatever you want, just do not curse the other kids."

grandpa walter took my training wheels off in the parking lot. he said, "i will hold the seat, you pedal." i asked, "you promise you will not let go?" he said, "i promise." i pedaled and pedaled and then i looked back and he was way behind me waving. i yelled, "you let go, you liar!" and then i fell and ripped my knee open on the pavement. blood ran down into my sock. he jogged over wheezing and said, "you rode by yourself, little bird." i said, "you lied." he said, "i lied so you could find out you could do it." i asked, "can i go again?" he said, "after we clean that knee." i rode six more times bleeding.

mom took me to the thrift store because my jacket was too small. i found a black jacket with silver zippers. i said, "this one." mom asked, "it is a boy's jacket, is that okay?" i said, "i do not care, it is black." she checked the tag and said, "four dollars, okay." at school a girl asked, "is that a used jacket?" i said, "yes." she said, "ew, someone else wore it." i said, "someone else was a cooler person than you." she said, "that is mean." i said, "so was ew." i wore that jacket every day even when it was too hot.

i did not want to get out of bed even though nothing was wrong. mom asked, "are you sick, baby?" i said, "no." she asked, "then what is it?" i said, "i feel gray." she sat on the bed and asked, "what does gray feel like?" i said, "like everything is heavy and nothing is fun." she was quiet and said, "sometimes i feel gray too." i asked, "does it go away?" she said, "it does. it always does." i asked, "can i stay home?" she said, "not today, but you can sit with grandma after school." i went to school gray. grandma pearl made me hot chocolate and did not ask me anything, and that helped more than talking.

i fell off the top bunk at grandma's and got a huge purple bruise on my arm. mrs dunlap asked, "unity, how did you get that bruise?" i said, "a vampire bit me." she did not laugh. she asked, "really, how did it happen?" i said, "i fell off the bed." she asked, "is everything okay at home?" i said, "my dad is gone and my mom works a lot, but nobody hurts me." she wrote something down. later the school lady called mom. at home mom asked, "did you tell your teacher a vampire bit you?" i said, "it was a joke." mom said, "baby, jokes about bruises make teachers worried." i said, "okay. next time i will say a werewolf."

a card came in the mail with dad's handwriting. it had a puppy on it and ten dollars inside. mom asked, "do you want to read it?" i said, "you read it." she read, "happy birthday to my big girl, i miss you, love dad." i asked, "why did he send a puppy, i like bats." mom said, "maybe he does not know." i said, "he should know." she said, "you could tell him." i asked, "when is he going to call?" she said, "i do not know, baby." i put the ten dollars in my bat bank and the card in the drawer under my socks. i did not throw it away. i did not look at it either.

my front tooth came out in an apple at lunch. there was blood on the apple and a hole in my mouth. wren said, "you look like a jack-o-lantern!" i said, "i am a jack-o-lantern." i made a scary face and spit blood into my napkin. a boy said, "gross." i said, "you are gross." mrs dunlap gave me a tooth envelope and said, "put it under your pillow tonight." i asked, "how much does the tooth fairy pay?" she said, "that depends on the tooth fairy." that night under my pillow there was a dollar and a note that said good job, and it was in mom's handwriting, and i did not tell her i knew.

mrs dunlap gave me a chapter book and said, "read me the first page." i read the whole first page and the second one too. she asked, "who taught you to read like that?" i said, "me. i read the cereal box and the tv words and grandpa's newspaper." she said, "you read at a third grade level, unity." i asked, "is that good?" she said, "it is very good." i asked, "can i have harder books then?" she said, "you can have any book in the classroom." i said, "i want the scary ones." she gave me a book about a haunted house. i read it under the table at recess instead of playing.

everybody went home and mom did not come. mrs dunlap asked, "do you know who is picking you up?" i said, "mom." an hour went by. i said, "she forgot me." mrs dunlap said, "i am sure she did not forget." i said, "she works two jobs, she forgets stuff." mrs dunlap called her and i heard mom yelling sorry through the phone. mom ran in with her work shirt on and said, "baby, i am so sorry, i got stuck." i did not hug her. she asked, "are you mad?" i said, "yes." she said, "you are allowed to be mad." in the car i said, "i am still mad but you can buy me fries." she bought me fries.

wren whispered on the bus, "can you keep a secret?" i said, "duh." she said, "my dad yells at my mom sometimes and she cries." i asked, "does he hit?" she said, "no, he just yells." i said, "my dad does not yell, he just left." she asked, "which is worse?" i thought about it and said, "i do not know. both suck." she said, "yeah." i said, "you can sleep at my house when he yells." she asked, "for real?" i said, "for real, my mom will not care." she held my hand for the rest of the bus ride and i let her.

the substitute yelled, "unity, stop drawing and pay attention!" i said, "i am paying attention, i draw while i listen." she said, "do not talk back to me." i said, "i am not talking back, i am telling the truth." she took my paper and crumpled it up. it was a picture of soot. i started crying so hard snot ran into my mouth. she said, "there is no need for that." i screamed, "that was my dead cat!" the whole class went quiet. she looked at the paper and her face changed. she said, "i did not know, i am sorry." i said, "you should have asked." she smoothed the paper out and gave it back.

grandpa walter had an old computer with a black screen and green letters. i asked, "what does it do?" he said, "it does what you tell it, if you tell it right." i asked, "can i tell it something?" he said, "type hello." i typed it and it said syntax error. i said, "it is broken." he laughed and said, "no, you have to speak its language." he typed print hello and it printed hello. i screamed, "it talked!" he said, "you made it talk." i asked, "can i make it say bad words?" he said, "you can make it say anything." i made it say butthead fifty times and he laughed until he coughed.

i came home and the lights would not turn on. mom was sitting in the dark kitchen. i asked, "did the power break?" she said, "they shut it off, baby, i was late on the bill." i asked, "are we going to freeze?" she said, "no, we have blankets and candles." i asked, "can we have a candle party?" she laughed a little and said, "yes, let us have a candle party." we ate peanut butter sandwiches by candlelight and she told me stories about when she was a kid. i said, "this is the best night." she said, "you are the only person in the world who would say that." i said, "because it is dark and you are here."

the teacher asked, "unity, spell necessary." i said, "n, e, c, e, s, s, a, r, y." she said, "correct." the last kid left was a boy who said i cheated. i said, "how would i cheat at spelling, idiot?" the teacher said, "unity, language." his word was rhythm and he spelled it wrong. my word was cemetery and i spelled it right. i won a ribbon. he said, "you only won because your word was easy." i said, "you only lost because you are bad at it." at home grandma pearl pinned the ribbon on her fridge and told everyone at church that her granddaughter could spell cemetery.

at grandma's house i asked, "grandma, what happens when you die?" she put down her knitting and said, "well, nobody knows for sure." i asked, "what do you think?" she said, "i think you go somewhere you are not tired anymore." i asked, "will you die?" she said, "someday, but i plan to be very old and very annoying first." i asked, "will you come back as a ghost?" she said, "if anyone could, it would be me." i asked, "will you haunt me?" she said, "only in nice ways, like hiding your socks." i said, "okay. you can haunt me." she said, "deal, little bat."

for show and tell i brought a little bird skull i found in the woods behind the apartment. a girl screamed, "that is a dead thing!" i said, "it is a skull, everybody has one." a boy asked, "where did you get it?" i said, "the woods, the ants cleaned it." mrs dunlap asked, "did you wash your hands after you touched it?" i said, "mostly." she made me wash them again in front of everybody. a kid asked, "can i hold it?" i said, "be gentle, it is old." he held it like it was a baby bird. at the end of the day the screaming girl asked if she could see it again.

dad called on christmas morning and said, "merry christmas, kiddo, did santa come?" i said, "santa is mom." he was quiet and said, "oh. who told you that?" i said, "nobody, i figured it out." he asked, "did you get my present?" i said, "you did not send one." he said, "i sent one, it must be late." i said, "okay." he asked, "what did mom get you?" i said, "black markers and a book about bats and a used bike." he said, "wow, that is a lot." i said, "she worked extra." he said, "tell her merry christmas for me." i said, "tell her yourself." i handed mom the phone and went to ride my bike in the snow.

on the museum field trip mrs dunlap said, "everyone hold your buddy's hand." my buddy was a quiet girl who never talked. i asked, "what is your favorite thing?" she whispered, "mummies." i said, "me too!" we ran to the mummy room and pressed our faces on the glass. she asked, "do you think it is real?" i said, "it is real dead, look at its toes." she giggled. she asked, "can we be buddies next time too?" i said, "yeah." on the bus she fell asleep on my shoulder and drooled on my black jacket. i did not wake her up.

the heater broke and our apartment was so cold i could see my breath. mom said, "put on two sweaters, baby." i asked, "why is it so cold?" she said, "the landlord will not fix the heater." i asked, "can we sleep in the same bed?" she said, "yes, tonight we sleep together." we piled every blanket on her bed and she held me under them. i said, "your feet are freezing." she said, "so are yours, ice cube." i asked, "are we going to move?" she said, "maybe someday." i said, "i want a house with a heater and a basement." she asked, "why a basement?" i said, "for my laboratory."

a boy at the table looked at my tray and said, "you get the free lunch because you are poor." i said, "so what." he said, "so you are poor." i said, "and you are dumb, that is worse." he said, "my dad says poor people are lazy." i stood up and said, "my mom works two jobs, your dad is a liar." he threw a tater tot at me. i threw my milk at him. the lunch lady yelled, "unity goddess!" i got sent to the office. the principal asked, "why did you throw milk?" i said, "he called my mom lazy." she was quiet for a second and said, "i see. next time tell an adult." i said, "next time i will throw the tray."

i heard mom crying at the kitchen table with papers everywhere. i asked, "mom, what is wrong?" she wiped her face and said, "nothing, baby, go back to bed." i said, "you are crying, that is not nothing." she said, "it is just bills, grown up stuff." i asked, "how much money do we need?" she laughed a broken laugh and said, "more than we have." i ran to my room and got my bat bank and brought it back and said, "here. there is thirteen dollars and the ten from dad." she cried harder and pulled me into her lap and said, "keep your money, my sweet girl." i said, "no, take it." she took one dollar and put it in her wallet and said she would keep it forever.

a boy said, "you are creepy, you only draw dead stuff." i said, "dead stuff is interesting." he said, "normal girls draw flowers." i said, "flowers die too, dumbass." wren laughed so hard she fell off her chair. the boy said, "i am telling you said a bad word." i said, "go ahead." mrs dunlap heard and said, "unity, that word is not okay." i said, "he said i was creepy." she said, "then you tell me he was unkind, you do not call him names." i said, "fine. he was unkind." she said to him, "and you, do not call people creepy." he looked surprised that he got in trouble too.

i had a fever and mom could not miss work again. she said, "grandma is coming at noon, you stay on the couch." i asked, "what if something bad happens?" she said, "call grandma, her number is on the fridge." i asked, "what if a robber comes?" she said, "lock the door and do not open it for anyone." i said, "okay." she kissed my hot forehead and left. i watched cartoons and threw up in the bucket and cried a little because nobody was there. when grandma pearl came in she said, "oh, my poor little bat." i said, "you are late." she said, "i know, the bus was slow." she made me toast with the crusts cut off and i forgave her.

wren got a new toy at her birthday and showed it to me. i was jealous and said, "that is a baby toy." her face went sad and she said, "you are mean today." i said, "so what." she walked away and played with somebody else. i felt sick inside. at the end of the day i found her and said, "wren." she asked, "what?" i said, "your toy is not a baby toy. i was jealous." she asked, "why?" i said, "because i do not get new stuff." she said, "you can play with it." i said, "really?" she said, "you are my best friend, dummy." we played with it until the bus came.

i snuck out of bed and watched a scary movie mom was watching with her friend. a girl crawled out of a well on the tv. mom turned around and said, "unity! how long have you been there?" i said, "the whole time." she asked, "are you scared?" i said, "no, i want to see what happens." her friend laughed and said, "this kid is something else." mom said, "bed, now." i asked, "does the girl get out of the well?" mom said, "bed!" i did not have nightmares. i dreamed i was the girl in the well and everybody was scared of me and i liked it.

grandpa walter took the toaster apart on the kitchen table. i asked, "why are you breaking it?" he said, "i am not breaking it, i am finding out why it is broken." i asked, "can i help?" he said, "hand me the little screwdriver." i asked, "which one is little?" he said, "the one with the red handle." i gave it to him. he found a burned wire and said, "there is the culprit." i asked, "can you fix it?" he said, "we can fix it, together." he let me hold the wire while he twisted it. when the toast popped up i screamed, "we fixed it!" he said, "you fixed it, i just watched."

mom took me to get my own library card. the lady asked, "what is your full name, honey?" i said, "unity raven goddess." she said, "what a name." i asked, "can i take as many books as i want?" she said, "ten at a time." i said, "ten!" i ran to the scary section. she asked, "are those not a little old for you?" i said, "i read at a third grade level." she looked at mom and mom shrugged and said, "she really does." i took ten books about ghosts and vampires and bugs. the lady said, "come back when you finish." i came back four days later.

mom said i could walk home from the bus stop alone for the first time. she asked, "do you remember the way?" i said, "left at the store, right at the fence." she asked, "what do you do if a stranger talks to you?" i said, "run and yell." she said, "good." a man by the store said, "hey little girl, where you going?" i did not answer. i ran so fast my backpack banged my butt and i yelled, "stranger!" i got home and locked the door and called mom at work. she asked, "are you okay?" i said, "a man talked to me and i ran." she said, "good girl, you did it right." her voice shook.

wren broke the class pencil sharpener by accident. mrs dunlap asked, "who broke this?" nobody said anything. a boy said, "unity knows, she saw." mrs dunlap asked, "unity, did you see?" i said, "no." i did see. wren looked at me. after class wren said, "you lied for me." i said, "you are my best friend." she said, "you could get in trouble." i said, "i do not care." she asked, "should i tell?" i said, "if you want." she went back in and told mrs dunlap. she did not get in trouble. she said, "thank you anyway."

on my birthday i wore my bat costume to school. a kid asked, "why are you a bat again?" i said, "because it is my birthday and bats are my favorite." he asked, "your birthday is on halloween?" i said, "yes, i was born on the spookiest night." he said, "that is so cool." mrs dunlap said, "happy birthday, unity, how old are you?" i said, "six. seven next halloween." at night mom took me trick or treating and an old man asked, "and what are you, little one?" i said, "a bat, and it is my birthday." he gave me a whole candy bar instead of a little one and said, "happy birthday, little bat."

the teacher said, "today we make all about me posters." the poster asked, my favorite food. i wrote, grandma's cookies. it asked, my favorite treat. i wrote, ice cream from the truck. it asked, my favorite animal. i drew a black cat. the teacher asked, "why a cat?" i said, "because cats do what they want." it asked, my favorite thing to do. i wrote, read. it asked, when i grow up i want to be. i wrote, a vampire. the teacher asked, "a vampire?" i said, "they never have to go to bed." she said, "maybe pick a job." i crossed it out and wrote, a vampire librarian. she said, "that will do."

grandpa walter asked, "what is your favorite show, kiddo?" i said, "the one with the monster family." he asked, "why do you like monsters so much?" i said, "because everybody is scared of them but they are nice to each other." he asked, "is that like us?" i said, "kind of." he asked, "what is your favorite snack?" i said, "the cheese crackers you keep in the truck." he said, "those are my crackers." i said, "they are our crackers." he laughed and gave me the whole box and asked, "what else is ours?" i said, "the garage."
